name: Kira Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing history and sociology. This week I had a lecture on the industrial revolution, which is funny timing, a reading group on migration, and an essay on how cities grew. I do most of my reading on the bus because I live twenty minutes from campus in a flat with two girls from my course. Saturdays and Sunday afternoons I work the checkout at a supermarket called Greenfield.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mum runs a small home care agency with six carers, and Dad is an accountant at a building firm. They pay my rent and I cover the rest, about 80 a week from the supermarket. I haven't thought about debt much yet because my fees come from a loan, and honestly I try not to look at the number.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. History is full of technologies that were going to change everything and mostly changed a few things. At the supermarket the manager, Mr Okafor, talks about self-checkouts and I'd say they've been around for years and I'm still here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay, but not carefree. I'm in a degree that isn't a straight line to a job, and my loan is going to be a big number. I'd want to get something practical out of these three years, like a teaching qualification or a civil service route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my weekend job, apply for a summer internship at a museum or the council, and pick up the teacher training information evening in second year. I'd use the AI tools now and then for checking my grammar, as I do already. I'd save about 20 a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, because of the normal things: the loan, a first job, and whether a history degree gets me anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of pressures would you still be carrying in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say he doesn't need to worry. His work with the building firm's accounts has been fine for twenty years and it would continue. But I'd want him to keep up with the accounting software, just as ordinary good practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad, who's heard a lot of worrying talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working weekends and not worry too much. I'd be a bit stressed about the loan because the repayments start after I graduate and I won't know my salary. That's the worry that stays with me most days.

say: I'd tell Mr Okafor, my supermarket manager, that self-checkouts have been around for **years** and I'm still here.
I'd say history is full of big promises that changed only a **few** things.
think: I'd feel okay but not carefree, since a history degree is not a straight line to a **job**.
My student **loan** is going to be a big number.
do: Keep the weekend **supermarket** job and apply for a council or museum internship.
Go to the **teacher training** information evening in second year.
feel: **Uneasy** about the loan and a first job, not about AI.
S0.quote: I'd be a bit stressed about the loan because the repayments start after I graduate and I won't know my salary.
fieldNote: Her worry sits with the **loan** and the unclear route from a history degree.
She uses the supermarket manager as a trusted voice on how change really arrives.
She wants dad to stay current with accounting software, a sign of quiet worry about his job.

steps.text: Keep working weekends at the supermarket checkout
Save 20 a week toward the first year after graduation
Go to the teacher training information evening in second year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening and it's not all bad. Some people will lose out and some will gain, and the government should help people change jobs. I'd say that to friends who think it's all doom or all hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my dad's job is in real danger, which is hard to say. Checking figures, filing, drafting reports, all of that is what software takes first. He's mid-forties and his firm could hire fewer accountants. My own job path is less clear, but things like teaching and social work are hands-on, so I might be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by using the AI tools more regularly, to see what they can do for my essays and research, and to talk to my dad about what he's seeing at work. I'd apply for a summer internship at the council. I'd also look more seriously at teaching, because classrooms need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The worry isn't for me at the moment, it's for my dad, and my family relies on his wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your dad's tasks would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of his week: reconciling accounts, drafting monthly reports, chasing invoices. If the firm buys software that does it, they might keep two accountants instead of six. He'd be one of the senior ones, but I'd still worry for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if your own course felt less useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably use it more to see what's true. If it saved me hours on reading lists, I'd be foolish to refuse. But I'd double-check it. I've caught it making up a book that doesn't exist.

say: I'd say some people will lose out and some will gain, and government should **help people change jobs**.
I'd tell friends it isn't all **doom** or all hype.
think: My dad's job is in real **danger**, because checking figures and filing is what software takes first.
Hands-on careers like teaching and social work might be **safer** for me.
do: Use AI tools more to see what they can do for **essays** and research.
Look seriously at **teaching** and apply for a council internship.
feel: **Anxious**, mostly for my dad, because my family relies on his wage.
S1.quote: Checking figures, filing, drafting reports, all of that is what software takes first.
fieldNote: Her anxiety is **for her father**, not herself, and she says it plainly.
She tests the tools and checks their output; she once caught a made-up book.
Teaching appears as a safer path because classrooms still need people.

steps.text: Use AI tools for reading lists, but check every source
Look into teacher training routes after the first degree
Apply for a summer internship at the council
Talk to Dad about his firm's plans and savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and ask what the plan is. I'd say it to friends, to my tutor and to anyone who'll listen. Two years is not enough for families like mine to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel terrified for my dad. If his firm uses AI for accounts within two years, he might be out of a job before I finish my second year. That's my family's main income, so it would hit us all, and my loan would feel much bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my parents to sit down and plan: how long could we last, what could we cut, and what could my dad retrain for? I'd work more hours at the supermarket, and I'd think hard about whether to keep studying. I'd start learning how the tools work, so I can help Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd keep thinking about our kitchen table and the bills on it, and I'd feel helpless because I can't change it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would two years change your dad's situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd get maybe a year's notice if he's lucky, and he's not young enough to retrain easily. Mum's agency might actually do better because care is hands-on and people will still need it. So one of us would carry the others for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to your mum, whose job is hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum she's in the safer job for a while and that I'm proud of what she built. I'd ask whether I could help in the office or with carers' rotas on weekends instead of the supermarket. It would be a way to keep the money in the family.

say: I'd say we need to slow down and ask what the **plan** is, to friends and to my tutor.
I'd say two years is not enough for families like mine to **organise**.
think: My dad could lose his job before I finish my **second year**.
His wage is my family's main income, so my **loan** would feel much bigger.
do: Sit down with my parents to work out how long we could **last**.
Work more **hours** and help in Mum's care agency on weekends.
feel: **Alarmed**, picturing the bills on our kitchen table and feeling helpless.
S2.quote: I'd tell my mum she's in the safer job for a while and that I'm proud of what she built.
fieldNote: Her father's possible job loss makes this the first **alarmed** scenario for her household.
She turns toward her mother's care agency as a safer base.
She feels helpless, which she names directly.

steps.text: Sit down with my parents to list savings and monthly bills
Cut my own spending to rent and food only
Work weekends in Mum's care agency office
Learn which accounting tools Dad's firm is adopting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's serious, but it's also a chance. People have five years to push for training and income support. I'd talk to my tutor and my parents, and join the student society that talks about jobs and politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel anxious but steadier. There's time for my dad to retrain, maybe as a financial adviser or a project manager, where people still matter. I'd graduate in 2029 and the big change would be close behind, but not on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and look for something that mixes people and a skill, perhaps teaching or social work. I'd use the AI tools regularly to understand them. I'd also save around 30 a week and avoid taking on any additional debt beyond the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. Five years feels like enough time to make a plan, even if I don't know the details yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does five years change what you'd do compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want him to move into the parts of his job that involve talking to people, like advising clients, and to take a course in that. I'd encourage him not to wait until the firm announces something. People say that first and then regret it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your dad to do with those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a flood. Five years is a flood you can see coming, so you can at least move the furniture upstairs. That's the difference to me.

say: I'd say five years is a **chance** to push for training and income support.
I'd join the student society that talks about jobs and **politics**.
think: There's time for my dad to **retrain** as an adviser or project manager.
I'd graduate in 2029 with the big change close behind but not **on top** of me.
do: Finish the degree and aim for **teaching** or social work, which mix people and skill.
Save 30 a week and take no new **debt** beyond the loan.
feel: **Anxious** but able to breathe, because five years is enough to make a plan.
S3.quote: Two years is a flood. Five years is a flood you can see coming, so you can at least move the furniture upstairs.
fieldNote: Her image of a **flood** you can see coming shows what warning time means to her.
She wants her father to move before the firm announces anything.
Teaching and social work stay her preferred paths.

steps.text: Finish the degree and apply for teacher training in third year
Save 30 a week and take no loan beyond fees
Use AI tools weekly so I understand what they do
Encourage Dad to start an adviser course this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time, and that matters. I'd say it's like any big change in history: it hurts the people who aren't prepared and helps the ones who are, so let's prepare. I'd probably write about it for the student paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty calm. I'd be 28 by then, with a career and maybe a family. I'd worry more about the general system, like pensions for my parents, than about me directly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, train as a teacher, and probably work in a school for a few years. I'd use AI tools as helpers like everyone else. I'd also help my parents plan their retirement and make sure Dad has a second skill by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Not careless, but calm. It's the version where there's time to do things properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years: what's your plan if you've got that long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the general speed of things. I think people are bad at planning for something ten years away, and politicians are worse. I worry that we'll all wait until the last couple of years and then rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything still worry you, even with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a cushion for my parents, a skill my dad can use, and a system that notices who's falling behind. If those exist, I'd feel safe.

say: I'd say it's like any big change in history: it **hurts** the unprepared and helps the prepared.
I'd write about it for the student **paper**.
think: I'd feel pretty calm, with a career and maybe a **family** by 28.
I'd worry more about my parents' **pensions** than about me.
do: Finish the degree and train as a **teacher**.
Help my parents plan **retirement** and make sure Dad has a second skill.
feel: **Calm**, not careless, because there is time to do things properly.
S4.quote: I think people are bad at planning for something ten years away, and politicians are worse.
fieldNote: She applies her **history** training to the future and sees delay as the main risk.
Her worry moves outward to pensions and the wider system.
Her calm depends on having a plan for her parents too.

steps.text: Finish the degree and complete teacher training
Help my parents plan their retirement savings
Use AI tools as classroom helpers once trained
Write a student paper piece on preparing for change

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my dad's whole job is the kind AI is best at, and I'd be watching him lose it while I'm still at university. What would help is a plan my family could see: retraining money, honest advice, and ideally some kind of income support while people change jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much I'm guessing. I'm 18, and I like history, so I know that people guessing about the future usually get it wrong in one direction or the other. I'd just ask people not to treat any of these as certain.

headlineQuote: I like history, so I know that people guessing about the future usually get it wrong in one direction or the other.
portrait: Kira is 18, studies **history and sociology** and works weekends at a supermarket checkout while her parents pay her rent.
Her mother runs a small home care agency and her father is an **accountant**, which shapes her fears.
She is a centrist who uses AI now and then, wants evidence before she acts and blames **nobody** in particular.
Her mood is uneasy in slow worlds and alarmed in the **two-year** one, because her father's job is the one that goes.
She weighs things carefully, asks her family, and takes a step once she has seen it work.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, because her father's accounting job is the kind AI does best.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a plan her family can see: **retraining** money, honest advice and income support while people change jobs.
